request: Why did repeat purchases drop this year?

questions.question: What decision will this help you make? For example: change a marketing campaign, adjust a loyalty offer, or report to leadership.
questions.why: Decision supported is the top priority and is unknown. Also frames what "repeat purchases" analysis needs.
questions.answer: We're deciding whether our retention efforts are working, and if repeat purchases have fallen, where to focus fixes. That will shape how we adjust our loyalty offers and what we report to the leadership team.

questions.question: How should we measure "repeat purchases"? Options: (a) the share of customers who placed a 2nd order within 90 days of their first; (b) the share of this year's buyers who had also bought before; (c) the number of orders from returning customers. Or tell me your own.
questions.why: Core KPI definition is ambiguous; need to pin it down before time range and breakdowns.
questions.answer: None of those quite fits. Use the share of customers who placed a second order within 12 months of their first order, grouped by the year of their first order.

questions.question: To find where to focus fixes, how should we split the repeat rate? Options: by the marketing channel customers came from, by product category of the first order, by customer age or gender, or by location. Pick any, or say "all".
questions.why: Breakdowns are needed; the stakeholder wants to know where to focus fixes.
questions.answer: Split it by location: the US on its own, then international by country.

questions.question: Who will read this dashboard: the leadership team, the loyalty/marketing team, or both?
questions.why: Audience unknown; affects level of detail.
questions.answer: Mainly the leadership team, since it's going into what we report to them. The loyalty and marketing team may look at it too, but leadership is the primary audience.

questions.question: Customers who first ordered in the last 12 months haven't had a full year to reorder yet. So 2026 can't be fully measured, and 2025 is only partly measurable. How should we handle it? Options: (a) show only customers with a full 12 months of history, so the latest complete group is first orders through September 2025; (b) also show 2025 and 2026 with a "not yet complete" label; (c) both, with the incomplete years shown separately.
questions.why: The 12-month cohort definition conflicts with "this year" (2026) given data ends Sept 2026; need a treatment decision.
questions.answer: I'd go with (c). I need to see 2026 to answer whether repeat purchases dropped, but leadership shouldn't read partial numbers as final, so keep the incomplete years visibly separate and labeled.

brief.business_question: How has the 12-month repeat purchase rate changed across customer groups by year of first order (2019 to 2026), and in which locations (US vs. each international country) is any change concentrated?
brief.audience: Leadership team (primary). The loyalty and marketing team may also use it.
brief.decision_supported: Whether retention efforts are working and, if the repeat rate has fallen, which locations to focus fixes on. This will shape loyalty offer changes and what is reported to leadership.

kpis.name: 12-month repeat rate
kpis.plain_definition: Of the customers whose first order was in a given year, the share who placed a second order within 12 months of their first order date. Customers are grouped by the year of their first order. A second order is a separate, later order by the same customer. Customers with only one order count in the base but not as repeaters.

kpis.name: First-time customers (group size)
kpis.plain_definition: Number of customers whose first order was in the given year. Shown so readers can see how big each group is. This is the base for the repeat rate.

kpis.name: Repeat customers
kpis.plain_definition: Number of those first-time customers who placed a second order within 12 months of their first order. This is the top of the repeat rate.

dimensions: Location: United States as one group, then international customers by country
brief.time_range: Customers by year of first order, from 2019 to September 2026 (the latest data). Complete groups (a full 12 months of history after first order) are shown in the main view. Incomplete groups are shown in a separate section, clearly labeled "not yet complete: not final".
brief.comparison: Year over year: each first-order year compared with earlier years. 2026 is compared with prior years, with a clear label that it is partial.
open_assumptions: 'Within 12 months' means the second order date is no more than 12 calendar months after the first order date.
Cancelled orders are not counted as orders (neither as first nor second order). Returned orders still count. Please confirm or change.
The first order is the customer's earliest order in the data. Customers who ordered before 2019 are not visible, so any who did would be wrongly treated as new in 2019.

Complete groups are customers whose first order was at least 12 months before the last date in the data (first orders up to September 2025). Because of this cut-off, 2025 is split: January to September 2025 is complete and October to December 2025 is incomplete. I assume the incomplete part of 2025 and all of 2026 go in the separate labeled section. Please confirm.

For incomplete groups, the rate uses only the time observed so far, so it will look lower than a full 12-month rate. It should not be read as a like-for-like drop. Please confirm this treatment, or ask for a same-elapsed-time comparison against earlier years.

Location is the customer's location on file (country, with the US shown on its own). It may not be where they lived at the time of the first order. Customers with a missing location go into an 'Unknown' group.
'This year' means 2026, based on data through September 2026.
out_of_scope: Explaining why repeat purchases changed. The data shows when and where the rate moved, not the cause. Any cause would be a hypothesis to test.
Judging whether loyalty offers or retention programs worked. The data has no record of loyalty offers, campaigns sent, or who received them. The dashboard can only show whether the repeat rate moved.
Final 2026 repeat rate. Most 2026 first-time customers have not had 12 months yet, so 2026 can only be shown as partial.

mappings.logic: Use the orders table (one row per order). Drop rows where orders.status = 'Cancelled'. For each orders.user_id, first order = MIN(orders.created_at). Count distinct user_id per first-order year and per location. Returned, Complete, Shipped and Processing orders all count as orders.

Using the same non-cancelled orders, join each customer's first order back to their other orders on user_id. A repeater has at least one different order_id with created_at later than the first order's created_at and no later than 12 calendar months after it. Count distinct user_id of repeaters. Add 12 months with a calendar-month function (for example DATETIME_ADD or DATE_ADD on the date), not a fixed 365 days.

Repeat customers divided by first-time customers for the same group (first-order year and location). One-order customers stay in the base. Calculate it from the sums of both counts, never by averaging rates across locations or years.
Take each customer's earliest non-cancelled orders.created_at and extract the year (UTC). This is a customer-level attribute that is fixed once per customer. It is not the year of each order.

mappings.item: Location: United States as one group, then international customers by country
mappings.logic: Left join the customer's first-order record to users on orders.user_id = users.id. Show 'United States' as its own group and each other users.country value as its own international group. If the user row is missing or country is null, label it 'Unknown'. 'España' and 'Spain' should be combined once approved.

Filter on the derived first-order year per customer. Apply it to the customer group, not to individual orders. Do not filter the orders table by year before finding each customer's first order and second order, or the second orders will be lost.
Filter on users.country, with 'United States' as the US option and an 'Unknown' option for missing values. Apply it after the customer's first and second orders are found.

mappings.item: Time range: 2019 to September 2026, complete vs not-yet-complete groups
mappings.logic: Customers are grouped by the year of their first order, from 2019 through 2026. The data ends at MAX(orders.created_at), 2026-09-30. A customer is in a complete group if first order <= (that end date minus 12 calendar months), so first orders up to 30 Sep 2025. Put complete groups in the main view. Put 1 Oct 2025 onward (Oct to Dec 2025 and all of 2026) in the separate 'not yet complete: not final' section. Set the flag for each customer, not for each year, because 2025 splits.

joins: orders.user_id = users.id (left join, to get users.country for each customer; keep customers with no matching user row as 'Unknown')
orders.user_id = orders.user_id (self-join on non-cancelled orders: first order to later orders of the same customer, with a different order_id)
order_items is not needed for this brief. The brief counts orders, not items or revenue.

gaps.reason: Data starts in January 2019 (first order 2019-01-13). Anyone who bought earlier looks like a new 2019 customer. This will inflate the 2019 group and may distort its rate. The data cannot identify these customers.
gaps.substitute: Label 2019 with this caveat. Optionally compare 2020 onward as the cleaner baseline.

gaps.item: Location at the time of the first order
gaps.reason: users holds one current country per customer. There is no address history or order-level country.
gaps.substitute: Use users.country as the location on file, as stated in the brief.

gaps.reason: users.country has both 'Spain' and 'España'. This is probably the same country spelled two ways. Counting them separately would split one country into two small groups. 'Brasil' appears only in that spelling.
gaps.substitute: Combine Spain and España into one group once the stakeholder approves. Otherwise show both as they are.

gaps.reason: The brief only asks for the observed-so-far rate, which is not like-for-like. A fair comparison needs a rate for earlier years over the same elapsed time. The data can support it, but it is not in the approved KPIs.
gaps.substitute: Show the observed-so-far rate with the 'not final' label. A same-elapsed-time version (for example, 6-month repeat rate across all years) could be added if approved.

gaps.item: Explaining why the repeat rate changed, and whether loyalty offers worked
gaps.reason: The data has no loyalty, campaign or offer records. It shows when and where the rate moved. It does not show the cause.

data_notes: Use orders (one row per order) for this brief. 'Second order' needs a different order_id, so counting order_items rows would wrongly treat a multi-item order as repeat purchases.

orders.status is the current status. An order that was returned after the order date still counts, as the brief says. A cancelled order is excluded as either a first or second order. If a customer's first order was cancelled, their first order becomes the next non-cancelled one, which may move them to a different year group.
Recent orders with status Processing or Shipped count as orders, since only Cancelled is excluded.

Data end date: orders.created_at ends 2026-09-30, but order_items.created_at goes to 2026-10-04 and returned_at, shipped_at and delivered_at go into October 2026. The brief uses order dates, so use the orders end date of 30 Sep 2026 for the cut-off.
The 12-month window is calendar months from the first order timestamp. Use created_at in UTC. Edge cases, such as a first order on 31 January, need one consistent rule from the date function.

Orders placed at the exact same timestamp as the first order, or on the same day, need a rule. Proposed: a second order is a different order_id with created_at strictly later than the first order's timestamp. A same-day second order counts. Please confirm.
users has 96,898 rows, but ids go up to 100,000. orders may reference user_ids missing from users. Those customers go to 'Unknown'. Check how many there are before launch.
The base only includes customers with at least one non-cancelled order. Registered customers who never ordered, and customers whose orders were all cancelled, are not in the base.

users.country is stored per customer and has 15 values. Some countries may have small groups in early years, so their rates will swing a lot. Show group size (first-time customers) beside every rate and consider a minimum-size flag.
users.first_name, last_name and email are personal data and must not appear on the dashboard. They are not needed here.
users.traffic_source and gender are not used by the brief. 'Customer groups' means year of first order only.

audit.summary: Four of the nine findings could distort the repeat rate. The worst are duplicate order IDs, orders with no customer, and orders dated in 2027–2028. The other issues are minor, and two are false alarms or expected (Kagawa/Kanagawa and Austria/Australia are real places, and shared emails don't matter here). Two items need a business decision: how to treat duplicate orders and orders dated in the future.

issues.explanation: Five orders are dated 2027 or 2028, but the data only runs to September 2026. These dates are impossible. If kept, they could be treated as a customer's first or second order. That would create fake repeaters, or put customers in a first-order year that does not exist. The true order date is unknown, so they can't be fixed.
issues.proposed_rule: Exclude orders with created_at later than the last valid data date (end of September 2026) from first-order and second-order logic. Log them in an exceptions list. Do not try to guess the correct date.
issues.decision_question: These 5 orders have dates in 2027–2028. We can't tell when they really happened. Is it OK to leave them out of the dashboard? It affects very few customers.
issues.rule: created_at must not be in the future

issues.explanation: Some order IDs appear more than once (5 rows affected). If these are the same order copied twice, a customer would look like they placed two orders. That would count them as a repeat customer by mistake. If they are two different orders sharing an ID, dropping one would lose a real order.
issues.proposed_rule: Check whether duplicate rows are identical (same user, date, status). If so, keep one row per order_id. If they differ, flag them and keep the earliest created_at row. Count distinct order_id when finding a customer's second order.

issues.explanation: Five orders have no customer attached. They can't be linked to anyone, so they can't count as a first or second order. They are very few, but they could make a customer's second order go missing.
issues.proposed_rule: Exclude orders where user_id is null from all customer-level calculations. Report the count of excluded orders.

issues.explanation: Five orders show 120 to 999 items, which looks like bad data. The repeat rate counts orders, not items, so item counts don't change it. These orders may be part of the same bad rows as other findings, so a check is still worthwhile.
issues.proposed_rule: Do not filter on num_of_item for this dashboard. Flag these orders and check whether they overlap with other flagged orders (future dates, duplicates, missing customer). Exclude them only if they do.
issues.rule: num_of_item more than 10x its 99th percentile (4), i.e. above 40

issues.explanation: Five orders show delivery before the order was created. This is impossible, so the delivery date is wrong. The repeat rate uses the order creation date, not the delivery date, so the KPIs are not affected.
issues.proposed_rule: Do not use delivered_at in this dashboard. Keep these orders, since created_at looks valid. Flag the rows for the data owner.
issues.rule: delivered_at must not be before created_at

issues.explanation: Five orders show delivery before shipping. Likely the same bad rows as finding 5. Shipping and delivery dates are not used in the repeat rate, so there is no impact.
issues.proposed_rule: none. Do not use shipped_at or delivered_at. Flag for the data owner.
issues.rule: delivered_at must not be before shipped_at

issues.explanation: Many rows share an email. The customer ID, not email, identifies a customer. In this kind of data, shared emails are common. The dashboard should count customers by user ID. Do not merge customers by email, because that would change group sizes.
issues.proposed_rule: none. Identify customers by user id, not email.
issues.rule: email should be unique per row

issues.explanation: Kagawa and Kanagawa are two different Japanese prefectures. This is not a typo. State is also not used, since location is shown by country.
issues.rule: rare spellings of a common value: 'Kagawa' looks like 'Kanagawa'

issues.explanation: Austria and Australia are two different countries. Merging them would put Austrian customers in Australia and distort the country view. Keep them separate.
issues.proposed_rule: none. Do not merge Austria into Australia.
issues.rule: rare spellings of a common value: 'Austria' looks like 'Australia'

time_window.explanation: Customers are grouped by the year of their first valid order, 2019 to 2026. Only orders created on or before 2026-09-30 are used, as that is the last valid order date. 12-month view: first order on or before 2025-09-30 is 'complete' (12 full months observed). First order from 2025-10-01 onward is 'not yet complete: not final'. So 2025 appears in both sections. 6-month view (same-time comparison): first order on or before 2026-03-31 has 6 full months observed. First order from 2026-04-01 onward is 'not yet complete: not final'.

shared_rules: Source is the orders table, one row per order. order_items is not used.

Valid order = status is not 'Cancelled', user_id is not null, and created_at is on or before 2026-09-30 23:59:59 UTC. Orders dated 2027 or 2028 are excluded and listed in an exceptions list. Returned, Complete, Shipped and Processing all count.
Duplicate order_id: if the duplicate rows are identical, keep one. If they differ, keep the row with the earliest created_at and flag it. Count distinct order_id throughout.
Orders with a null user_id are dropped from all customer calculations. The count is reported in the exceptions list.
Apply the exclusions above BEFORE finding each customer's first order. So a customer whose first order was cancelled gets their next valid order as the first order.
First order = the customer's valid order with the earliest created_at (UTC). Tie on the same timestamp: the lowest order_id is the first order.
Customer group = year of the first order (UTC). It is set once per customer. Never filter orders by year before finding first and second orders.
12-month complete flag is set per customer: 'Complete' if first order created_at is on or before 2025-09-30 23:59:59. Otherwise 'Not yet complete: not final'.
6-month complete flag is set per customer: 'Complete' if first order created_at is on or before 2026-03-31 23:59:59. Otherwise 'Not yet complete: not final'.

Location = users.country on file, from a left join on orders.user_id = users.id. 'United States' is its own group. Every other country is its own group. 'España' is merged into 'Spain'. A missing user row or null country becomes 'Unknown'. All ~15 countries are shown, no limit needed.
Ratios are always computed as sum of repeaters divided by sum of first-time customers. Never average rates across locations or years.
Every rate is shown beside its group size. Groups with fewer than 50 first-time customers carry a 'small group: rate may swing' flag.
The 2019 group is labeled: 'may include customers who first ordered before 2019, as data starts in Jan 2019'.
No personal data (name, email) appears on the dashboard. delivered_at, shipped_at and num_of_item are not used.

metrics.name: First-time customers (group size)
metrics.question_answered: How many customers made their first order in each year, and in each location?
metrics.formula: Count of distinct user_id among valid customers, grouped by first-order year, completeness flag and location. Each customer is counted once, in the group of their first valid order.
metrics.grain: One row per first-order year x completeness flag x location. A second set of rows gives 'All locations' per year and flag, summed from the location rows.
breakdowns: Completeness flag (complete / not yet complete: not final)
Location (United States, each other country, Unknown)
metrics.time_logic: Place each customer by the year of their earliest valid orders.created_at (UTC), 2019 to 2026. Complete flag: first order on or before 2025-09-30. Not yet complete: first order from 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-30.
cleaning_rules: Customers with no valid order are not in the base (never ordered, or all orders cancelled).
metrics.excluded_example: A customer whose only order is Cancelled is not counted. A customer whose only order is dated 2027 is not counted.

metrics.name: Repeat customers
metrics.question_answered: How many first-time customers placed a second order within 12 months of their first order?
metrics.formula: Count of distinct user_id where the customer has at least one other valid order (different order_id) with created_at strictly later than the first order's created_at and on or before first order created_at + 12 calendar months. Use a calendar-month function (e.g. DATETIME_ADD(..., INTERVAL 12 MONTH)), not 365 days. A same-day second order counts. Because only orders up to 2026-09-30 exist, not-yet-complete groups only count seconds observed so far.
metrics.grain: One row per first-order year x completeness flag x location, plus 'All locations' rows per year and flag (summed).
metrics.time_logic: Customer is placed by first-order year (created_at, UTC). The second order must fall in the window (first order, first order + 12 calendar months]. The window is also cut at 2026-09-30.
cleaning_rules: Second order must be a different order_id. Duplicate rows of the same order_id do not create a repeater.
Returned orders count as second orders. Cancelled orders do not.
metrics.excluded_example: A customer whose second order came 13 months after the first is not a repeater. Nor is one whose only other order is Cancelled.

metrics.name: 12-month repeat rate
metrics.question_answered: What share of each year's first-time customers ordered again within 12 months, and where has it moved?
metrics.formula: Repeat customers divided by first-time customers for the same group (first-order year x completeness flag x location). One-order customers stay in the base. For 'All locations' rows, divide the summed repeaters by the summed first-time customers.
metrics.grain: One row per first-order year x completeness flag x location, plus 'All locations' rows per year and flag. Columns: first-time customers, repeat customers, rate, small-group flag.
breakdowns: Location (United States, each other country, Unknown)
metrics.time_logic: Same as the two counts. Main view: complete customers only (first order 2019-01-01 to 2025-09-30), so 2025 here means Jan-Sep 2025. Separate section: first orders 2025-10-01 to 2026-09-30, labeled 'not yet complete: not final'. These rates only use time observed so far and are not like-for-like with complete groups. Readers are pointed to the 6-month repeat rate for a like-for-like view.
cleaning_rules: If a group has no first-time customers, show the rate as blank ('no customers'), never 0%. Such rows are not charted.
Flag groups under 50 customers as small.
metrics.excluded_example: A customer who first ordered on 2025-11-10 is not in the main view. They appear only in the 'not yet complete: not final' section.

metrics.name: 6-month repeat rate (same-time comparison)
metrics.question_answered: Using the same 6-month window for every first-order year, did the repeat rate really drop in recent groups such as 2026, and where?
metrics.formula: Customers whose first-order year, flag and location match the row AND who have at least one other valid order (different order_id) with created_at strictly later than the first order's created_at and on or before first order created_at + 6 calendar months, divided by first-time customers in the same row. Use a calendar-month function (e.g. DATETIME_ADD(..., INTERVAL 6 MONTH)), not 180 days. One-order customers stay in the base. For 'All locations' rows, divide summed 6-month repeaters by summed first-time customers. Columns: first-time customers, 6-month repeat customers, 6-month rate, small-group flag.
metrics.grain: One row per first-order year x 6-month completeness flag x location, plus 'All locations' rows per year and flag (summed).
breakdowns: 6-month completeness flag (complete / not yet complete: not final)
Location (United States, each other country, Unknown)
metrics.time_logic: Customer is placed by first-order year (created_at, UTC). Second order must fall in (first order, first order + 6 calendar months], also cut at 2026-09-30. Main like-for-like view: first orders 2019-01-01 to 2026-03-31, so 2026 here means Jan-Mar 2026 only. Separate section: first orders 2026-04-01 to 2026-09-30, labeled 'not yet complete: not final' (these have under 6 months observed and will look lower).
cleaning_rules: Second order must be a different order_id. Returned orders count as second orders. Cancelled orders do not.
If a group has no first-time customers, show the rate as blank ('no customers'), never 0%. Such rows are not charted.
Flag groups under 50 customers as small.
metrics.excluded_example: A customer whose second order came 8 months after the first is not a 6-month repeater, though they count as a 12-month repeater. A customer who first ordered on 2026-05-15 is not in the main 6-month view.

decisions_assumed: 'Within 12 months' = second order is later than the first and no later than first order + 12 calendar months (UTC timestamp). Edge dates such as 31 Jan follow the date function's rule consistently.
'Within 6 months' for the same-time comparison follows the same rule with 6 calendar months.
The 6-month view is complete for first orders up to 2026-03-31. So 2026 in the like-for-like view covers January to March 2026 only. April to September 2026 is shown separately as not final.
The 6-month rate is shown for every first-order year, 2019 to 2026, next to the 12-month rate.
A same-day second order counts, if it is a different order_id with a strictly later timestamp.
The 5 orders dated 2027 or 2028 are excluded and logged. Their true dates are unknown.
Duplicate order_ids are collapsed to one row (earliest created_at if they differ).
The 5 orders with bad item counts or bad delivery dates are kept. Neither field is used.
'España' is merged into 'Spain'. 'Brasil' stays as its only spelling.
Customers with a missing user row or null country go into 'Unknown'. Their count is checked before launch.
Location is the country on file, not necessarily where they lived at first order.
12-month complete = first order on or before 2025-09-30, set per customer. So 2025 is split: Jan-Sep complete, Oct-Dec not yet complete.
2026 is partial in the 12-month view and shown only in the not-yet-complete section. 'This year' = 2026 through 2026-09-30.
2019 may include customers who first ordered before 2019. It is shown with a caveat. 2020 onward is the cleaner baseline.
Small-group flag threshold is 50 first-time customers.
Empty groups (no customers) show a blank rate, not 0%.
Customers who never ordered or only have cancelled orders are not in the base.
Cause of any change and loyalty offer impact cannot be answered. The data has no offer or campaign records.

sql.sql:
WITH dedup AS (
  SELECT order_id, user_id, status, created_at
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.orders`
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY created_at ASC) = 1
),
valid AS (
  SELECT order_id, user_id, created_at
  FROM dedup
  WHERE status != 'Cancelled'
    AND user_id IS NOT NULL
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01')
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-01')
),
first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, created_at AS first_order_at
  FROM valid
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at ASC, order_id ASC) = 1
),
u AS (
  SELECT id, country
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.users`
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY created_at ASC) = 1
),
cust AS (
  SELECT
    f.user_id,
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM f.first_order_at) AS first_order_year,
    IF(f.first_order_at < TIMESTAMP('2025-10-01'), 'Complete', 'Not yet complete: not final') AS completeness_flag,
    CASE
      WHEN u.country IS NULL OR TRIM(u.country) = '' THEN 'Unknown'
      WHEN u.country = 'España' THEN 'Spain'
      ELSE u.country
    END AS location
  FROM first_orders f
  LEFT JOIN u ON u.id = f.user_id
),
by_loc AS (
  SELECT first_order_year, completeness_flag, location,
         COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS first_time_customers
  FROM cust
  GROUP BY first_order_year, completeness_flag, location
),
combined AS (
  SELECT * FROM by_loc
  UNION ALL
  SELECT first_order_year, completeness_flag, 'All locations' AS location,
         SUM(first_time_customers) AS first_time_customers
  FROM by_loc
  GROUP BY first_order_year, completeness_flag
)
SELECT
  first_order_year,
  completeness_flag,
  location,
  first_time_customers,
  IF(first_time_customers < 50, 'small group: rate may swing', 'ok') AS small_group_flag,
  IF(first_order_year = 2019, 'may include customers who first ordered before 2019, as data starts in Jan 2019', '') AS year_note
FROM combined
ORDER BY first_order_year, completeness_flag, location = 'All locations', location

WITH dedup AS (
  SELECT order_id, user_id, status, created_at
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.orders`
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY created_at ASC) = 1
),
valid AS (
  SELECT order_id, user_id, created_at
  FROM dedup
  WHERE status != 'Cancelled'
    AND user_id IS NOT NULL
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01')
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-01')
),
first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, created_at AS first_order_at
  FROM valid
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at ASC, order_id ASC) = 1
),
u AS (
  SELECT id, country
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.users`
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY created_at ASC) = 1
),
cust AS (
  SELECT
    f.user_id,
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM f.first_order_at) AS first_order_year,
    IF(f.first_order_at < TIMESTAMP('2025-10-01'), 'Complete', 'Not yet complete: not final') AS completeness_flag,
    CASE
      WHEN u.country IS NULL OR TRIM(u.country) = '' THEN 'Unknown'
      WHEN u.country = 'España' THEN 'Spain'
      ELSE u.country
    END AS location
  FROM first_orders f
  LEFT JOIN u ON u.id = f.user_id
),
by_loc AS (
  SELECT first_order_year, completeness_flag, location,
         COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS first_time_customers
  FROM cust
  GROUP BY first_order_year, completeness_flag, location
),
combined AS (
  SELECT * FROM by_loc
  UNION ALL
  SELECT first_order_year, completeness_flag, 'All locations' AS location,
         SUM(first_time_customers) AS first_time_customers
  FROM by_loc
  GROUP BY first_order_year, completeness_flag
)
SELECT
  first_order_year,
  completeness_flag,
  location,
  first_time_customers,
  IF(first_time_customers < 50, 'small group: rate may swing', 'ok') AS small_group_flag,
  IF(first_order_year = 2019, 'may include customers who first ordered before 2019, as data starts in Jan 2019', '') AS year_note
FROM combined
ORDER BY first_order_year, completeness_flag, location = 'All locations', location

WITH dedup AS (
  SELECT order_id, user_id, status, created_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY created_at ASC, status) AS rn
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.orders`
),
valid_orders AS (
  SELECT order_id, user_id, created_at
  FROM dedup
  WHERE rn = 1
    AND COALESCE(status, '') != 'Cancelled'
    AND user_id IS NOT NULL
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01')
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-01')
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT user_id, order_id, created_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at ASC, order_id ASC) AS rn
  FROM valid_orders
),
first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, order_id AS first_order_id, created_at AS first_created_at,
         TIMESTAMP(DATETIME_ADD(DATETIME(created_at, 'UTC'), INTERVAL 12 MONTH)) AS window_end
  FROM ranked
  WHERE rn = 1
),
users_clean AS (
  SELECT id,
         CASE
           WHEN NULLIF(TRIM(country), '') IS NULL THEN 'Unknown'
           WHEN TRIM(country) = 'España' THEN 'Spain'
           ELSE TRIM(country)
         END AS location
  FROM `analyst-agent-512103.thelook_dirty.users`
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY id) = 1
),
customers AS (
  SELECT f.user_id,
         EXTRACT(YEAR FROM f.first_created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AS first_order_year,
         IF(f.first_created_at < TIMESTAMP('2025-10-01'), 'Complete', 'Not yet complete: not final') AS completeness_flag,
         COALESCE(u.location, 'Unknown') AS location,
         EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM valid_orders v
           WHERE v.user_id = f.user_id
             AND v.order_id != f.first_order_id
             AND v.created_at >= f.first_created_at
             AND v.created_at <= f.window_end
         ) AS is_repeat
  FROM first_orders f
  LEFT JOIN users_clean u ON u.id = f.user_id
),
loc_counts AS (
  SELECT first_order_year, completeness_flag, location,
         COUNT(*) AS first_time_customers,
         COUNTIF(is_repeat) AS repeat_customers
  FROM customers
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
),
all_locations AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT location FROM users_clean
  UNION DISTINCT SELECT 'Unknown'
),
grid AS (
  SELECT y AS first_order_year, fl AS completeness_flag, l.location
  FROM UNNEST(GENERATE_ARRAY(2019, 2026)) AS y
  CROSS JOIN UNNEST(['Complete', 'Not yet complete: not final']) AS fl
  CROSS JOIN all_locations l
  WHERE (fl = 'Complete' AND y <= 2025)
     OR (fl != 'Complete' AND y >= 2025)
),
by_location AS (
  SELECT g.first_order_year, g.completeness_flag, g.location,
         COALESCE(c.first_time_customers, 0) AS first_time_customers,
         COALESCE(c.repeat_customers, 0) AS repeat_customers
  FROM grid g
  LEFT JOIN loc_counts c
    ON c.first_order_year = g.first_order_year
   AND c.completeness_flag = g.completeness_flag
   AND c.location = g.location
),
combined AS (
  SELECT first_order_year, completeness_flag, 'All locations' AS location, 0 AS location_sort,
         SUM(first_time_customers) AS first_time_customers,
         SUM(repeat_customers) AS repeat_customers
  FROM by_location
  GROUP BY 1, 2
  UNION ALL
  SELECT first_order_year, completeness_flag, location,
         IF(location = 'United States', 1, IF(location = 'Unknown', 3, 2)) AS location_sort,
         first_time_customers, repeat_customers
  FROM by_location
)

  first_order_year,
  completeness_flag,
  location,
  first_time_customers,
  repeat_customers,
  SAFE_DIVIDE(repeat_customers, first_time_customers) AS repeat_rate,
  IF(first_time_customers < 50, 'small group: rate may swing', '') AS small_group_flag,
  IF(first_time_customers = 0, 'no customers', '') AS no_customers_note,
  IF(first_order_year = 2019, 'may include customers who first ordered before 2019, as data starts in Jan 2019', '') AS cohort_note
FROM combined
ORDER BY first_order_year, completeness_flag DESC, location_sort, location

spec.notes: Definitions I applied (please confirm): (1) A repeat customer has at least one other valid order, with a different order_id, placed within 12 calendar months of their first order (inclusive). (2) Duplicate order_ids are collapsed (earliest created_at kept) before the validity filter. (3) Valid = not Cancelled, user_id not null, created 2019-01-01 to 2026-09-30 UTC. First order found after these filters. (4) Rows are built on a full grid of year x flag x location so empty groups show a blank rate; combos that cannot exist (e.g. 2026 Complete) are left out. 2025 appears twice: Jan-Sep as Complete, Oct-Dec as 'Not yet complete: not final'; 2026 is only in the not-yet-complete section. Not-yet-complete rates use only the time observed so far and are not like-for-like. Use the 6-month repeat rate for a fair comparison. 'All locations' rows sum repeaters and first-time customers. España is merged into Spain; missing user or country is 'Unknown'. The exceptions list (2027/2028 orders, null user_id counts) is not part of this query. No personal data is output.

         COALESCE(u.location, 'Unknown') AS location,
         EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM valid_orders v
           WHERE v.user_id = f.user_id
             AND v.order_id != f.first_order_id
             AND v.created_at >= f.first_created_at
             AND v.created_at <= f.window_end

  LEFT JOIN users_clean u ON u.id = f.user_id

findings: The repeat rate has not fallen: the 12-month rate rose from 10.9% for customers whose first order was in 2019 to 19.3% for 2024 and 24.5% for January–September 2025.

2026 does not show a real drop: the 19.1% 12-month figure for 2026 is not final because those customers have had little time to reorder, while the like-for-like 6-month rate for January–March 2026 first orders is 20.2%, against 15.0% for 2025.

There is no location where a fall is concentrated: from 2024 to 2025 the 12-month rate rose in every country with a sizeable group, for example the US from 20.0% to 23.7% and Japan from 15.9% to 25.7%.

The US, Brasil and Belgium have the lowest 2025 rates among the larger locations (23.7%, 23.8% and 23.4%), and the UK had the smallest gain (22.6% to 24.8%), so these are the places with the least recent improvement.

Read with care: 2019 may include customers who ordered before the data starts, October–December 2025 (28.1%) and April–September 2026 (17.2% over 6 months) are not final, and the data cannot show why the rate moved or whether loyalty offers had any effect.
